analysis.one_liner: Requires automatic shutoff valves, public disclosure of pipeline hazards, and first-ever carbon dioxide pipeline safety rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote: introduced in August 2024 with zero cosponsors, it sat in two House committees until the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require pipeline companies to install automatic valves that shut off ruptured pipelines within 30 minutes, publish what substances run through pipelines near homes, and alert residents and first responders. It would create the first federal safety standards for carbon dioxide pipelines, prohibit blending hydrogen into ordinary gas lines until Congress regulates it, set up an office within the federal pipeline safety agency to help communities file complaints and get help after leaks, and let private citizens sue pipeline operators that violate safety rules. It would also bar people with financial stakes in pipeline, petroleum, or gas companies from serving on the industry advisory committees that help write federal pipeline safety standards.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live, work, or go to school near large gas, hazardous liquid, or carbon dioxide pipelines — especially those in 'high consequence areas' where a rupture could be deadly. The bill would give them rupture-actuated shutoff valves, annual notices about the pipes near their homes, public websites with hazard data, and trained local emergency responders. Communities of color and low-income communities near pipeline infrastructure would get a dedicated federal office to help them file complaints and seek compensation after incidents.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents near major pipelines and first responders

how_it_helps.text: Operators of covered pipelines in populated or high-consequence areas would have to isolate a ruptured segment within 30 minutes and demonstrate that ability within 5 years, with waivers only after public notice and consultation [S2].

Operators would have to publish, free of charge, what substances they transport, incident and repair history, pressure limits, emergency plan excerpts, and — for carbon dioxide pipelines — modeled fatality zones; owners, tenants, and first responders would get annual written notice of their legal rights [S2].

The Secretary would have to write the first minimum safety standards for carbon dioxide pipelines, including leak-detection odorants, rupture-zone modeling, geohazard assessment, and training for local emergency responders, responding to the 2022 Denbury pipeline rupture investigation [S2].

PHMSA would create an Office of Public Engagement to coordinate outreach, complaint handling, translation, and post-incident remediation help, with funding authorized at $12 million per year for fiscal 2025-2028 [S2].

Members of the technical safety standards committees who are chosen from the public could no longer have financial interests in the pipeline, petroleum, ethanol, or gas industries, and would have to submit financial records to prove it [S2].

Private citizens could sue pipeline operators — and the government when it fails to perform nondiscretionary duties — for civil penalties and injunctions, and a prohibition would bar releasing reportable quantities of gas or hazardous liquid [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Pipeline operators — gas transmission, hazardous liquid, gathering, and carbon dioxide pipelines — would bear the cost of retrofitting rupture-mitigation valves, building public disclosure websites, sending annual notices, and paying higher civil penalties. Some of those compliance costs would likely be passed to customers through rates, and the bill authorizes roughly $1.1 billion in new federal grant spending (fiscal 2027-2031) plus the public engagement office.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pipeline operators, gas customers, and federal taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The compliance burden — valves, disclosure systems, annual notifications — would fall on pipeline operators, and some of it would likely be recovered from customers through rates [S2].

The bill would allow waiver of the 30-minute isolation rule where compliance is 'operationally, technologically, or economically infeasible', a flexibility critics could point to as a gap in the mandate [S2].
It would prohibit any hydrogen blending in ordinary gas distribution lines until Congress acts, which could halt utility hydrogen pilot projects even where operators argue they are safe [S2].

It would strike several existing statutory cost-benefit requirements for pipeline safety rulemaking, shifting the agency's legal framework toward safety and climate factors and away from cost tests — a change industry groups would oppose as potentially expensive and legally contested [S2].

The bill authorizes new federal spending: $200 million per year for fiscal 2027-2031 for the natural gas distribution grant program plus $48 million for the public engagement office, adding to federal outlays [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people living near large pipelines, the safety and right-to-know provisions address a real and documented risk — the bill's carbon dioxide section is written around a specific 2022 rupture investigation. The main cost is compliance spending by pipeline companies, some of which would reach customers through bills, plus new federal grant spending. The bill is broadly drafted and would impose costs industry-wide rather than targeting the worst operators, but it includes waivers where compliance is infeasible.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure and Energy and Commerce committees on the day it was introduced, then sent to a subcommittee, and neither committee ever acted on it before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Lori Trahan introduced the bill in the House on August 6, 2024, near the end of the two-year congressional session [S1].
No members of either party cosponsored the bill [S3].
The Speaker referred it to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and the House Energy and Commerce Committee [S4].

The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials, where it stayed; no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action followed before the Congress ended [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pipeline and gas companies came out ahead: they avoided rupture-shutoff requirements, public hazard disclosure, citizen lawsuits, and first-ever carbon dioxide pipeline safety rules by the bill dying without any committee or floor action.

for.name: Rep. Lori Trahan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as its sole sponsor; no other member joined as a cosponsor.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and sent the bill to its Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials Subcommittee; never held a hearing or markup.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received a referral of the bill's provisions within its jurisdiction; never acted on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no member of either party cosponsored the bill, so the partisan split was never tested; the sole sponsor was a Democrat.

industries.industry: Pipeline operators (gas transmission, hazardous liquid, gathering, and CO2 lines)
industries.note: The bill would require rupture-mitigation valves isolating ruptures within 30 minutes, public disclosure of hazard data, incident reporting, a ban on reportable releases, higher exposure to penalties, and private lawsuits. These costs fall on companies whose releases endanger the communities near their lines.

industries.industry: Gas utilities and local distribution companies
industries.note: They would gain extended access to a $200 million-per-year federal grant program for repairing, retiring, or replacing distribution pipes, with prevailing-wage and apprenticeship incentives — but the bill would also prohibit blending hydrogen into their systems until Congress acts and push 20% of grant funds toward non-emitting alternatives like electrification.

industries.industry: Carbon capture and carbon dioxide pipeline developers
industries.note: The bill imposes the first federal minimum safety standards, odorant, rupture-zone modeling, and emergency-response requirements on carbon dioxide pipelines; clear federal standards could also give the emerging carbon transport industry a stable regulatory foundation to build on.

Pipeline safety rulemaking would have to weigh the need to mitigate climate impacts and avoid prolonging fossil fuel infrastructure life, and grant funds would shift toward non-emitting alternatives, nudging federal policy away from extending fossil fuel systems.
